title: The Lamp at Harbor Point
chapters: Joon spun round when an old boat entered Harbor Point Museum. The sky began to brighten up after a night of rain. Mina used a cup to bail water out of the boat. Mr Han glossed over damage on the wooden side, but Mina marked it in her notebook. She tried to buck Joon up because their summer job had started badly. At the back of the boat, Joon found a weather book tucked away in a box by a seat. The book held a map, a key, and a photo of a metal lamp. A name on the photo had been covered with a black mark.

Joon tucked his shirt in and carried the book to the office. Mr Han brewed up tea for the three of them. The museum had chalked up a hundred visitors during the recent holiday. A city committee now planned to clamp down on places with weak roofs. Mr Han invited Mina and Joon to dine out at a local restaurant after work. During dinner, he dredged up a memory of his father, Leo Han. Leo had operated a signal house on the high hill. Mr Han had closed the house after an accident and had never returned.

The museum engine suddenly keeled over and stopped the lamps. Mina and Joon knuckled down to the difficult repair job. A private company wanted the land, but Mr Han would not knuckle under to the demand. Joon perked up when the lamp case became visible in the daylight. Mr Han reeled off dates from the town history without checking a text. Mina and Joon spruced up the main gallery with fresh paint and a new display. The photo in the weather book showed the same lamp. A line on the page it referred to a rescue during an ancient storm.

Mr Han asked Joon to give over making jokes about ghosts. The two students could get around town on bicycles. Mina cut a newspaper article out of an old magazine. Joon put the hot lamp glass by the window to cool down. Mr Han began to open up about Leo's final year at the signal house. Mina cut across the museum garden to find a file in the office. The file showed a business offer from West Shore Company. The director wanted to replace the museum with a hotel.

Mina filled in a form for the city record office. She and Joon planned to sleep over at Sara's family home by the harbor. The evening bus would call at the record office on the path. A missing permit had set back the museum repair. Sara looked over the old map with great care. Mina did not want to put Sara out, but she needed help through the night. Sara was a university student with knowledge of local architecture. She saw that one corner of the map had been cut away.

Joon needed time to take in the complex message in Leo's book. Repair costs had gone up during the year. Mr Han put Mina forward for a youth position on the museum committee. The committee agreed to bring in an engineering expert. Mina looked to the weather record for proof. The expert told Joon to back off from the damaged lamp wire. A storm warning appeared on the radio. Harbor Point had three days to prepare for severe rain.

A visitor blocked the car in at the museum gate. Mina and Joon checked into a cheap hotel because Sara's apartment was full. Joon walked off after Mina accused him of losing the map corner. They met at the harbor wall and made up. Mina asked the way that they should go about finding the missing paper. Joon agreed to go along with Mina as she interviewed old citizens. They went back to the hotel and compared the map with a modern road guide. A blue mark pointed from the museum to the coast.

The summer job had already become difficult work. Mina had expected a quiet museum, but she now faced a private company, a damaged building, and a family secret. Joon created a digital copy of the map. The map used a small scale. Sara measured the lamp case and recorded the material, height, and weight. Mr Han prepared a public statement about the roof condition. The committee requested a detailed budget, an expert opinion, and a safe repair schedule. Mina saw an opportunity to protect the museum, but she also understood the risk. Their opening task was to learn the truth about the signal house.

On the same afternoon, Ms Park arrived with her husband and son. The quiet lady was the new public partner for the repair. She chose a spot by the main desk and began to consider the situation. She actually knew the company agent, and her sense of risk told her that he would probably seek a quick deal. Her international experience gave the staff a broad view. She would suggest a public model in that the whole town could receive a voice. A couple from the city offered space for a meeting. Ms Park asked Mina to raise the concern and develop the idea through steady effort.

Mr Han showed Ms Park a film made during the last century. The film was a useful source on wood, oil, gas, and heat in the signal house. Natural damage could cause a fire, so their concern was quite serious. A common repair method would certainly improve the structure, but the museum had to make a choice. The work might cost a thousand dollars and increase at a rapid rate. Mina examined the figure and said, 'I can check the bill myself.' Mr Han smiled because her simple promise made the heavy problem feel easy.

West Shore sent an agent that claimed that a court would accept the private deal. He said the company could produce jobs, earn capital, and offer credit to the customer. Ms Park replied that the citizen deserved freedom to join the debate. Her strategy was to establish a public base and prevent a company attack. If the museum failed to manage the repair, the hotel plan might achieve popular support. If the town worked as one, the impact could bring success. Mina saw that the summer job now had a clear purpose.

Mina knew exactly the place to apply the new plan. A male graduate at the university campus had built an instrument that could predict the consequence of a fuel spill. His secretary arranged a proper appointment despite the short time. The main difficulty was travel, because traffic around the campus was extremely heavy. Joon said they could possibly wait, but Mina preferred to act. She truly believed the hill was in risk, even if West Shore called the fear a novel idea.

The graduate opened a silver chest and removed a tool for testing tree roots. A small shadow on the sample meant that the land was hardly clean. The result was basically an emergency for the ground zone of the hill. The beauty of the landscape made the hidden damage more painful. The graduate refused cash and said he would appreciate public credit for the work. 'We must protect this place ourselves,' Mina said. The contrast between the green hill and the dark sample made Joon quiet.

The visitors had to go away from the harbor road as rain made it dangerous. Mina wanted to get away from the hotel early. Joon's rage could not take away the benefit of his help. Sara put down the phone after arranging an interview. An old fisherman agreed to put them up for one night. Mina's camera ran out of power during the call. She charged it at the hotel and packed a raincoat. The three left for the west side of town.

At the bus stop, Sara asked them to hold on while she checked the address. Joon had to stand in for Mina during a short radio interview. Mina picked up a box from the record office. They went round some homes and spoke with elderly citizens. A story about Leo worked Joon up, and he became impatient. Mina called up Mr Han for a direct answer. He admitted that Leo had argued with the company owner about the hill land. He did not explain the reason that the map had been hidden.

Mina feared that she would let Mr Han down. The record office officer let her off the usual copying cost. Joon let on that he had found a letter in the weather book. The letter could turn the committee against Mr Han. The students started off for the house of the fisherman at noon. Leo had started out as a boat mechanic and later became the signal expert. His letter claimed that West Shore Company had missed a safety report. Mina wondered if Mr Han had covered up that fact.

A dog ran after their bicycles on the sea path. Sara ran the interview questions over with Mina. Joon shouted, Watch out! A branch fell across the road. The group believed that proof would win out and overcome the false story. Mina hoped to win the fisherman over with an honest account. The fisherman had once bought into a small boat business with Leo. He remembered the night of the accident clearly. A rescue boat had reached the harbor because Leo's lamp remained bright.

The students stayed out late and listened to the fisherman. The effect of Joon's rage began to wear off. The fisherman refused to cover up Leo's mistake: Leo had left the signal house during the storm. A senior officer had stepped down after the accident. Mina wanted time to relax, but Sara said they had to push on. A black car followed them, and they tried to shake it off on a narrow lane. The car finally entered the highway. Joon wrote the number on his hand.

At the house, Joon kicked off his wet shoes. The fisherman spelled out the full rescue story. Sara asked after his wife, and he said she was in hospital. Joon did not talk back when Mina told him to listen. Years of sea wind had worn the window frame down. The accident threw them together, and they became companions. The fisherman played an old tune, and everyone sang along. He said West Shore had cooked up a false report about Leo.

Joon almost chickened out of reading Leo's letter. Mina called Mr Han, but he rang off when she mentioned the company. Sara kicked up a serious protest about his quiet. The final fact from the fisherman bowled Mina over: Leo had not abandoned the signal house. A company truck had taken him away after he reported an illegal fuel tank. The missing map corner might show the tank site. At midnight, Mina heard a vehicle in the open the house. The black car had returned.

The man left a blank envelope at the door and disappeared. In was a recent photo of the signal house. A red circle marked the broken roof, and a printed message warned them to stop. Sara regarded the message as a threat and contacted the police. Mina examined the paper, print style, and black mark. Joon saw the company mark in a pale background image. The officer asked them to preserve the proof and avoid the hill until morning. Mina agreed, but she knew the storm would arrive soon.

A local author had recently given the fisherman a tape with the title The East Wind. Upon hearing the sound, Mina knew that one scene had a source in Leo's radio. The original voice was familiar, and the calm expression was similar to Mr Han's. A short stop on the tape could indicate a change, while a soft word might reveal the hidden source. Sara used a computer screen to examine the exact moment when Leo stopped speaking during the old film. A dark mark covered Leo's lip. The recording did not represent the complete event. Mina refused to accept a lie without context, but she also waited for Leo's full response.

The fisherman said the company had influence because the story was easy to repeat. Since the accident, citizens had regarded Leo's name as a problem instead of a real man. Joon felt rage, but Mina reminded him that an angry attitude could create trouble. The challenge was to reflect the fact without an attack on somebody. Their specific method required a wide search, a bit of calm, and the power to perform careful work. Indeed, the truth itself might be a plain story, but it could prevent real harm.

The blank message made Sara wonder if somebody planned to steal the deal. She wanted to pursue the black car, but the officer told them to stay in. Joon called the whole mystery crazy and began to complain in a loud manner. Mina had serious doubt about the man, but she did not regard the stranger as an enemy. The fisherman said a true hero did not act without thought. His calm advice surprised Joon and changed the mood in the room.

To keep busy, they helped their host prepare a small public notice. The page had a column for the local association and a separate space for the age and gender. A golf club offered to host a championship, while a fashion group planned a simple show. Mina opposed an event that would divide the town or tie support to wealth. The fishing group promised an enormous meal instead. Unfortunately, the plan could not succeed unless the museum found a safe place for the crowd.

The fisherman dished up eggs, bread, and hot soup at morning. Joon washed down the bicycle wheels and removed the mud. Sara flagged up a weather change on her phone. Mina did not brush the warning off. She brushed up on the old map symbols with the fisherman. West Shore wanted the missing corner too, so the group chose to go after it in daylight. Their search would go beyond the normal museum job. A police car followed at a safe length.

Joon rode fast and got ahead on the field path. The police permit helped their plan get past the officer at a locked farm gate. The fisherman knew of a spring at the back of the hill. Mina thought the path through. Only then could anyone cross the bridge. The old map began to come apart in the rain. Their small shelter wanted for a strong roof. Joon promised not to tell on Mina for tearing the map. The hospital called Sara away from the group. She tried on a bigger raincoat and left with the police car.

Mina asked for a short delay, then began climbing. Joon owned up to hiding Leo's letter from her. The hotel put a call through to Mr Han. Mina and Joon talked their debate out by the road. They chose to start over with full trust. Mr Han planned to start up the museum radio and guide them from town. Mina heard from Sara that the wife of the fisherman was well. Joon played back a recorded message from Leo's old radio.

The message described families that had moved away after the accident. West Shore had moved into the empty boat yard. Leo had lived through the storm but lost his job. A safety rule had been written into the land deal. Mina sat down on a rock and read the exact line. Joon sat through the full legal account without a joke. The line ended with a promise to keep public access to the hill. Mina chose to stand against West Shore's private hotel plan. She would rather protect the hill.

Two old paths met up at the spring. Mina and Joon set about matching rocks to the map. Joon set off a small alarm in the police safety box by accident. They set up a rain shelter by a rock. The sky changed back from dark to blue for a moment. Mina watched over the weather book while Joon searched. A young oak had grown to a surprising height by the old bridge. Finding the corner could win back public control of the hill. They cut through thick grass and reached a rock wall.

A weak animal needed care, and Joon stopped to care for it. The delay gave Mina time to notice a box mark on the wall. Their meeting at the spring broke up, and the group took three paths. The wet climate did not agree with Joon's injured ankle. Water had worn away the paint on the box mark. Mina found a small box at a shop that had closed up. She fired off a message to Mr Han with the place. Joon threw away a broken plastic cover from the box.

The rain grew strong, so Mina helped Joon bed down in the shelter. She pushed aside her fear and opened the metal box. The box held the missing map corner and a copy of the land deal. A signature appeared on the copy. The city mayor would need to push the document through a public hearing. The old signal machine could save on power by using the lamp mirror. Mr Han would have to answer for hiding the deal. Mina and Joon arrived at a difficult result: he had protected his father, but his quiet had also helped the company. They checked the papers over and placed them in a dry envelope.

The hill gave them a powerful view of the coast. A wave hit the rocks as Mina compared the map with the wild land itself. The marked range had the shape of a bird, and one narrow line ran east to a small beach. Joon found a land sample in the box. A scientific note said that fuel could destroy plant life across a wide area. Mina thought of the planet, not only the town, and wanted to explore the damaged spot. The warning seemed impossible to prove during a storm, but the old trees had managed to survive.

Sara called with additional facts from a university report. The average temperature on the hill had risen by one degree, mostly because the tree cover had changed. The land still had an advantage: the basic water system could easily support young plants. A quick plan could encourage families to protect the hill and learn a local tradition. Joon said the plan lacked money. Mina replied that the museum could earn support by giving citizens a real feature to see. The land deal was not only legal stuff; it was a plan for life.

The fisherman had once worked as a tourist guide, and he knew the landscape on the far side of the hill. He described a valley. A rare creature lived there in a smooth rock shell. A long journey would bend to the opposite coast, then lead elsewhere through a silver field. Joon wanted to bury the wet papers in his coat and continue, but Mina told him to concentrate. The path was roughly double their planned length. A leather belt around the document box held perfectly, and the inner pages stayed dry.

A teenager from a junior nature club met them by a fence. She carried an essay about the unknown plants on the hill. Her principal had advised the club to communicate with visitors and share local wisdom. The girl quietly said that the company had told her group to quit the survey. Mina felt pride and joy at her power. Her cheek was cut by a branch, but she did not seem mad. She and Joon could disagree about the path and still work as one team.

A stream sprang from the rock by the shelter. The top part of the path began to ice over. Joon wanted to hide away until the rain stopped. Fallen leaves blocked the stream up and sent water to them. Mina began to warm to the idea of using the signal house. She rang round the police, museum, and harbor office for help. Joon breathed in slowly and stood. A strong wind knocked the supply box over. Mr Han told them to lock up the signal house and place the documents in the metal case.

The long path made them land up at the signal house by evening. Mina rolled out the map on a wooden table. Police marked the dangerous floor off with a red line. A rescue truck pulled out of the town yard and entered the road. Sara sent the land deal in to Ms Reed's office by email. Mr Han promised to serve his duty out and tell the committee everything. The signal house could serve up a clear signal for boats if they repaired it. The short time worked Mina up. Everyone had to speed up the work while light remained.

The repair plan began to fall apart when the mirror wheel would not move. Joon fell for a false arrow painted on the wall. Mina refused to pass up the chance to test the real handle. The adults and students pulled together around the wheel. A rescue member acted the process out. Police tracked down a missing machine part in a floor box. Mr Han tore down a weak board on the machine. Sara printed out Leo's steps from the museum file.

The company director suddenly rounded on Mr Han by phone. Mina led off the reply with the land line. Mr Han admitted that a university had sent him down during his student years for hiding proof in a student case. Despite that old event, he helped Joon pull through the pain in his ankle. Mina had to tear herself away from the debate and focus on the storm. The company tried to freeze Mr Han out of the land meeting. Joon had finally wised up to the reason for Mr Han's fear. The music group tuned up for the harbor radio show.

The committee had passed Mr Han over for a director role, but control of the lamp had passed to him from Leo. The group decided on the most simple repair. Sara singled Joon out for finding the machine part. Mina acted on the weather advice from the harbor. They guarded against broken glass with coats and gloves. Joon married up the paper lines with numbers on the wheel. The pieces fit together, and the mirror began to turn. Mr Han asked everyone to shut up for the radio call.

The harbor office marked the signal as ready. A young rescue member wanted to rush into the rain, but Sara stopped him. The sight of the bright mirror knocked the company director out during the video call. A digital control could lock the light into the harbor system. Families packed into the safe half of the signal house. Mr Han's old story did not square with the deal, and Mina asked for the full truth. The secret dragged Sara in and harmed her trust. Mina insisted on an open statement after the storm.

Joon stretched out on a blanket while Sara checked his ankle. Mina laid the weather book out by the controls. A metal point stuck out from the lamp stand. The old rescue story began to stir up public interest. Everyone wrapped up in dry coats. Sara watched Ben switch off during Mr Han's long account and begin to sleep. The shame of that old event had dragged Mr Han down. Mina stopped him from dragging old blame up during the rescue. West Shore might fold the hotel plan up if the land line became public. Mr Han did not rise to West Shore's angry message. A possible answer occurred to Mina: use the old lamp to guide the rescue boat.

The control software had one useful feature, but the old screen showed only a weak line. Sara used extra tape to hold a wire in the appropriate shape. Joon tested the machine twice and found that the lamp could use half power. The repair was not complete, and they had little time for an exchange of ideas. Hey! Joon asked Mina for a tool when a loose part began to shake. Mina hated his wild tone, but the fear on his face was obvious. She reminded herself that a team could improve only when a member could speak.

The machine needed a target, so Mina marked the rescue boat on the map. Perhaps the storm had moved it somewhere far from the usual channel. The group could not see the boat, and the radio had nearly lost power. Mr Han was certain that the lamp could reach it, while Sara said the chance was probably small. Mina simply asked everyone to try. The team placed themselves around the wheel, and Mina kept the radio by herself. Their shared effort gave the old machine a new life.

An electric motor in the lamp began to make an awful rhythm. Joon opened a battery cover and found a broken string around the drive belt. A repair guide from the garage said to adjust the load and test the function. Sara used a rope to lift the wheel, while Mina gave the metal a gentle bend. A remote control did not work, so Joon had to invent a direct wire. The wheel began to shine, and everyone was greatly pleased. Mina admired Joon's talent, though she still worried about his toe and injured ankle.

For one sudden moment, the light stopped and the room became a scene from a horror film. Joon pretended to be confident, but even he looked afraid. An old clue on the machine showed a new power line in the stair. Mina begged Mr Han to wait while Sara checked it. He said that experience had made him wise, not brave. The team had to relax enough to think. They found the fault, joined the wire, and watched the lamp return with a brilliant white light.

The fishing boat remained at sea, and the risk hung over the room. Sara firmed up the radio plan with the harbor officer. The public team beat off West Shore and won control of the rescue boat. A safe hour was slipping away. Mina slipped the code into her radio message. Mr Han straightened out the mirror problem. He had carved out a work life at the museum despite that old event. Joon peeled off his wet socks and stood at the wheel.

West Shore had tried to carve the hill up for private houses. The director clammed up when the mayor asked about the deal. A city officer told him to hush up and listen to the rescue channel. The storm could push a weak boat into the open sea. The director finally yielded to the public access rule. The mayor promised to rein in plan costs. Mina tried to soften the director up by explaining the museum benefit. He attempted to fob her off with a short answer.

Sara rustled up a meal from bread, soup, and fruit. West Shore could not get round the clear land law. A fallen tree made the rescue truck turn back. Members threw damaged boards out of the signal house. The director could not buy the officer off, and the officer recorded his offer. The city had cut the museum budget back for three years. Mina looked through Leo's weather pages for a path on the map. A farmer dropped in and described a field road. The rescue team set fuel aside for that distant path.

News of the old lamp began to take off online. Mr Han chose to go back to the museum and bring the lamp case records. The power of the students blew the harbor members away. Mina fought back when fear tried to stop her, and she held the radio steady. Mr Han gave control of the mirror to Joon. Sara did Joon's boot up and checked his ankle. The group ate the soup up and waited for the new radio call. At midnight, the truth about the company offer came out on local news.

Mr Han tried to bear up as press team asked about Leo. Mina asked him to move over so she could speak. Sara rang the meal cost up on the museum account. The fisherman came round to the signal house with a dry coat. The rescue team had little fuel but could get by. Mina left details out of her public statement. Harbor prices had bottomed out after the storm warning. Her clear words gave the members power. A young expert lived in the signal house for the night to operate the lamp.

Joon could not see the appeal Mina saw in the damaged old building. The harbor office stepped up rescue work as the boat radio became weak. Ben threw in a useful question about the tide. Mina took on the job of reading Leo's signal numbers. They found out that the last number pointed to a safe channel. Nobody gave up as the wind grew strong. Sara marked the channel on the map. The team followed the new direction, and the rescue boat found the fishing boat. In the morning, the two boats entered Harbor Point.

The town met the team at the harbor hospital. A doctor regarded cold hands, a nurse examined a wounded fisherman, and Sara recorded the medical result for the family. Mina felt comfort, but she also knew a public conflict was coming. The mayor scheduled a hearing for Monday. West Shore hired a professional agent and published a negative statement. Mr Han prepared to admit his quiet. Joon promised to support the museum with proof instead of emotion. The lamp had saved lives again, but the future of the hill remained uncertain.

The rescue captain said the boat had been close to the rocks when the light struck the water. The light gave the team a new direction and helped them survive. One fisherman had apparently seen the light, while citizens on the boat were busy with a broken motor. Mina did not know if the lamp by itself had saved them. Anyway, the event showed that old knowledge could work with modern skill. The captain promised to remind the hearing that a public signal could protect many affairs.

At the hospital, one fisherman felt ill and held his stomach. A nurse gave him a pill and checked the raw cut on his hand. The captain told Mina that the storm had felt like an adventure only after it ended. During the worst episode, the team member had a new job. One fisherman had been a fighter, one had carried the heavy load, and one had kept the radio alive. The rescue was partly skill and partly fortune. Their joy grew gradually when the test result was clear.

The mayor tried to quiet the room at the Monday hearing. Nobody would cast Mr Han out until he spoke. The company accepted the demand for a public record. The committee agreed to limit private building on the hill. Mr Han's honest statement changed the view of some critics. The agent tried to fool the audience with a map that was not complete. Sara quickly made copies of the full deal. Mina explained that a business could not get round the access law.

At the hearing, the chairman gave a female student the opening question. Mina spoke about the nation, local freedom, and the benefit of international experience. She said a museum should exist for the public, especially for a child that could not travel. A large crowd listened as she explained the purpose of the signal house. The director tried to change the subject, but the mayor asked him to answer. The public influence in the room was powerful, and his money was weak. The committee chose a plan that felt the two practical and fair.

The committee president asked whether the town was able to meet the repair cost. The current tax plan had little money available, and the economy was sometimes weak. An annual term would involve a cost of one pound per visitor. The mayor hoped to reduce that amount through a public fund and a national resource plan. The financial authority had to determine whether the plan met the general standard. At least everyone agreed that the public would gain a permanent benefit.

A researcher showed a series of maps on sea movement. The southern region had lost land, and the loss was particularly clear at the edge of the hill. A sea wall could protect one surface but affect water elsewhere. Thus, the entire plan needed a broad treatment plan, not one quick wall. The researcher explained the sort of risk and showed a method for removing polluted land. Her positive result gave the room hope.

The university theory used a pattern in the plant cell. Fuel on the skin of a root could prevent a plant from developing, while a clean finger of land could contain life. Plants tended to respond well when citizens maintained the land. The examine did not assume that one technique would solve the problem. It offered a basis for more work. Mina saw that science could directly support the land deal.

The insurance department said a private firm could not own public rescue property. A previous rule gave the museum an independent status during a crisis. The chief officer recalled a victim that had suffered during an old storm. None of the company plans had provided an effective mission for public safety. The officer stared at the director and asked him to deny that fact. He could not.

The mayor immediately announced a public session and invited the citizen to attend. A local press team entered the studio and prepared to release the debate live. The press member intended to define the legal term without changing it. A device on the table displayed the voting score. The room became completely quiet when Mina walked to the table. Her presence carried the spirit of the harbor.

Mina said justice required a lasting answer, not only victory in a fight with one company. Democracy worked only when citizens could participate and accept duty. A folk group, a church, and an eastern mosque had contributed to the rescue meal. Their religions differed, but they shared the principle of public care. The town could engage a broad variety of citizens without placing a border around belonging. The crowd began to understand her vision.

The director tried to grab the radio and comment on his desire for a hotel. The chairman said he was responsible for the annual safety report and could not deny the missing page. Ms Park demonstrated a change West Shore had made to the limit on the company map. A small change had hidden an important aspect of the deal. Citizens were obviously aware of the trick now. West Shore's status began to fall.

The mayor asked the two sides to combine their useful ideas and settle the case. The museum would extend the public path, promote local work, and repair the facility. West Shore could contribute clean material but would not own land. The offer was relatively fair, and the company eventually accepted it. A new category of protected land would emerge from the deal. Mina felt the relation between old days and the future become clear.

The committee turned the hotel plan back. It rejected the false safety report. Police charged the director with offering money to an officer. The city chose to cut private support back and repair the museum. Mina looked through the budget and found a useful grant. A university professor dropped in with an offer of help. The committee set money aside for the signal house. Public interest grew after the rescue story. Mr Han could finally go back to work without hiding Leo's name.

A thunderstorm crossed the northern edge of town during the night. It broke the museum phone network and left the chess club without a meeting room. The rain did not stop the individual from offering help, nor did the dark. Mr Han was absolutely certain that the museum would open. The walls were generally dry and only slightly damaged. One ancestor of the fisherman had built the old light, so the family arrived and repaired it.

The county had to locate money so the museum could expand. It was currently unable to obtain a large grant because the town carried old debt. Ms Park proposed a public bond and asked families to invest a small amount. The selection board wanted a brief account of the expense. Mina prepared it and proved that the town could acquire material without waste. The board approved the plan.

Mina wanted the building to support mental care as well as history. A quiet garden could surround visitors with flowers and give a tired soul room to breathe. The committee chose to adopt the notion and connect it to a public aid. Mr Han somehow found space at the back of the west wall. He had to acknowledge that Mina's unique idea was practical. The group concluded that the museum would shift largely to public care.

A designer opened a large sheet and marked the length, depth, and angle of a new wing. Industrial steel would support the roof, while solid iron would hold the lamp platform. Members filled a floor gap with sand and attached a sharp edge cover. A tube would control water flow into a storage area. The part had to work within the building capacity. The design gave the old space a strong new form.

The plan had to ensure equal access and eliminate a high step at the door. A typical conservative design would retain the step, but Mina refused. Meanwhile, Sara confirmed that a smooth path would help a visitor with a chair. The committee frequently relied on old practice, but this change was entirely needed. The new door would attract more families. Even the team accepted the appeal.

West Shore tried to reject the public bond and launched an ad to oppose it. The company declared that the museum could not defend the cost. Mina used the rescue record to convince worried citizens. A proud supporter spoke about the museum reputation, while a company member began an aggressive protest. Tension rose until Ms Park asked the two sides to negotiate. They resolved the debate without a shout, and the protest became silent.

The university lab prepared a medical display with a safe model of the breast, muscle, hip, and internal tissue. It explained surgery and showed that a genetic change might affect a cell. A virus section showed that clean hands aid healing. The display used pure material and avoided a sharp surface. A pregnant visitor and a blind visitor tested the path. Their comments helped the team improve the room design. One characteristic still needed work.

The science wing also examined space far from Earth. A distant satellite sent an electronic picture of the atmosphere, and a model showed the vast universe. One experiment followed the water cycle from a dark sky to a crop. A giant storm was an extreme phenomenon, but local weather could also change rapidly. The display connected the disaster to the natural origin. Mina was definitely surprised by the clear picture.

The harbor room followed boxes from an airline station to the port. A small vessel carried a fishing net, while a bigger ship moved food to cold storage. Visitors could transfer a box, check it, and distribute it to a shop. The task appeared simple but was complicated. If one machine crashed, the entire line had to adapt. Joon bet that he could finish quickly, but the boxes went nowhere when he missed a code.
